--- title: "Model Comparison and Averaging" bibliography: stat-mod.bib csl: conservation-biology.csl --- ::: {.cell} ::: ## What predicts species richness best? ***Temperature*** or ***Human Impact***? ::: {.fragment} We saw that including both in one model had problem of collinearity ::: ::: {.fragment} But does one predict richness better than another? ::: ::: {.fragment} We cannot use LRT because these are not nested models, in fact they have the same d.f. ::: {.columns} :::: {.column} $$ \begin{aligned} \log(\mu_\text{spp richness}) &= b_0 + b_1 \log(\text{area}) + b_2 \text{temperature} \\ \log(\mu_\text{spp richness}) &= b_0 + b_1 \log(\text{area}) + b_2 (\text{human impact}) \end{aligned} $$ :::: ::: ::: ## This is a job for AIC ***Akaike Information Criterion*** $$ AIC = -2 \mathcal{l}(\hat{\theta}_{MLE}) + 2k $$ - $\mathcal{l}(\hat{\theta}_{MLE})$ is max of the log likelihood - $k$ is number of parameters ::: {.fragment} We can compare non-nested models with AIC ::: ## This is a job for AIC $$ AIC = -2 \mathcal{l}(\hat{\theta}_{MLE}) + 2k $$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_temp <- glm.nb(nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + avg_temp_annual_c, data = dat_plt) AIC(mod_temp) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2321.152 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mod_hii <- glm.nb(nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + hii, data = dat_plt) AIC(mod_hii) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2314.374 ``` ::: ::: The human impact model is better supported (lower AIC) ## This is a job for AIC $$ AIC = -2 \mathcal{l}(\hat{\theta}_{MLE}) + 2k $$ Purpose of $2k$ term is more clear for models with unequal d.f. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_temp_precip <- glm.nb( nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + avg_temp_annual_c + rain_annual_mm, data = dat_plt ) AIC(mod_temp_precip) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2297.937 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} AIC(mod_hii) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2314.374 ``` ::: ::: Now the `temp + rain` model is better supported ## AIC penalizes more parameters But... ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} logLik(mod_temp_precip) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'log Lik.' -1143.968 (df=5) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} logLik(mod_temp) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 'log Lik.' -1156.576 (df=4) ``` ::: ::: adding parameters will always increase log likelihood ::: {.fragment} Is the increase real? Or just *"over fitting"* ::: ::: {.fragment} *"over fitting"* is a term for what we know already: more parameters could let a model wiggle to fit noise ::: ## AIC penalizes more parameters How? and why? ::: {.r-stack} :::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out} Imagine you have one data set ::: {.columns} :::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](aic-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column} and fit a model to it by maximizing likelihood. :::: ::: :::: :::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out} Imagine you have one data set then collect a new one ::: {.columns} :::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](aic-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column} and calculate the log likelihood of the new data given the same model fit to the first data :::: ::: :::: ::: ## AIC penalizes more parameters How? and why? ::: {.r-stack} :::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out} Imagine you have one data set ::: {.columns} :::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](aic-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column} and fit a model to it by maximizing likelihood. :::: ::: :::: ::: ## AIC penalizes more parameters How? and why? Imagine you have one data set then collect a new one ::: {.columns} :::: {.column} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](aic-slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=576} ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column} ::: {.r-stack} :::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out} We could calculate the log likelihood for the new data ***but*** with parameter estimates from original model :::: :::: {.fragment} The difference between the mean log likelihood of the original data and the mean log likelihood of the new data will be about $k$ :::: ::: :::: ::: ::: {.absolute top="70%" left="35%" style="z-index: 10;"} ::: {.fragment} $$ \frac{1}{n} \mathcal{l}(\hat{\theta} \mid \text{data}_\text{orig}) - \frac{1}{n} \mathcal{l}(\hat{\theta} \mid \text{data}_\text{new}) \approx k $$ ::: ::: ## AIC penalizes more parameters

So AIC is trying to account for the chance that additional parameters are just fitting noise by including a penalty for those additional parameters ## Returning to model comparisons We can rest assured that the improvement in AIC for the `temp + rain` model is not due just to adding antother parameter ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} AIC(mod_temp_precip) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2297.937 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} AIC(mod_hii) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2314.374 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} A common rule is that models with AIC values within 2 points are effectively equivalent; $>2$ means one model really is better supported [@burnham-anderson] ::: ## Model averaging ::: {.incremental} - model comparisons tells us which model is more supported, a way of testing hypotheses - model averaging is less about testing hypotheses and more about ***prediction*** - for example: how can we best predict tree richness across the pae ʻāina? ::: ## Model averaging Consider the 3 models we have made so far ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + hii nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + avg_temp_annual_c nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + avg_temp_annual_c + rain_annual_mm ``` ::: ::: {.fragment} Each model makes a different prediction about the expected number of species in a plot ::: ::: {.fragment} How could we combine the models to make one prediction? ::: ::: {.fragment} Why do we want to? ::: ## Model averaging Consider the 3 models we have made so far ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + hii nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + avg_temp_annual_c nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + avg_temp_annual_c + rain_annual_mm ``` ::: The predictions from the combined model will be more accurate than any one model by itself ::: {.fragment} And also better than one big model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + hii + avg_temp_annual_c + rain_annual_mm ``` ::: Because we know, e.g., there are issues of collinearity. *For smaller data sets over fitting one big model is also an issue* ::: ## Model averaging How do we combine models to make one prediction? ::: {.fragment} We could average the parameters of each model to make an ***average*** model $$ \begin{aligned} \log(\mu_\text{nspp}) = &b_0^{\text(avg.)} + b_1^{\text(avg.)} \log(\text{area}) + b_2^{\text(avg.)} \text{hii} + \\ &b_3^{\text(avg.)} \text{temp} + b_4^{\text(avg.)} \text{rain} \end{aligned} $$ where, e.g., $b_3^{\text(avg.)}$ is the *average* of all slope estimates for `avg_temp_annual_c` across all the models ::: ## Model averaging Let's make that more concrete with our actual models. ::: {.fragment} Here are the slope estimates for temperature in every model where it shows up ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coefficients(mod_temp)["avg_temp_annual_c"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` avg_temp_annual_c 0.02427288 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} coefficients(mod_temp_precip)["avg_temp_annual_c"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` avg_temp_annual_c 0.02797484 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} ::: {.cell} ::: So the average slope is $b_3^{\text(avg.)} = \frac{0.024 + 0.028}{2} = 0.026$ ::: ## Model averaging Note: there are two ways to average ::: {.columns} :::: {.column} average over ***only models*** where the variable shows up
$b_3^{\text(avg.)} = \frac{0.024 + 0.028}{2}$ :::: :::: {.column} average over ***all models*** no matter if the variable shows up
$b_3^{\text(avg.)} = \frac{0 + 0.024 + 0.028}{3}$ :::: :::
::: {.fragment} The default in the code we'll use for model average is to use ***only models*** where the variable shows up ::: ## Model averaging But this simple average parameter value ignores the fact that some individual models are already better at making predictions ::: {.fragment} The AIC values tell us about the support of each model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} AIC(mod_hii) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2314.374 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} AIC(mod_temp) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2321.152 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} AIC(mod_temp_precip) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2297.937 ``` ::: ::: ::: We want to account for these differences in support when averaging ## Model averaging We turn AIC values into weights. For model $i$: $$ w_i = \frac{e^{-\Delta\text{AIC}_i / 2}}{\sum_j e^{-\Delta\text{AIC}_j / 2}} $$ where $\Delta\text{AIC}_i = \text{AIC}(\text{model}_i) - (\text{minimum AIC})$ ::: {.fragment} The weights sum to 1, they can be roughly interpreted as the probability that $\text{model}_i$ is the best supported model ::: ## Model averaging Again, let's make this concrete ::: {.columns} :::: {.column width=33%} $\text{AIC}_i$ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} AIC(mod_hii) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2314.374 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} AIC(mod_temp) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2321.152 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} AIC(mod_temp_precip) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2297.937 ``` ::: ::: :::: :::: {.column width=33%} $\Delta\text{AIC}_i$
16.438
23.216
0 :::: :::: {.column width=33%} $w_i$ ::: {.cell} :::
0.00027
0.00001
0.99972 :::: ::: ## Package *MuMIn* does this for us! Create the averaged model ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(MuMIn) # pass in a list of all models we want to consider mod_avg <- model.avg(list(mod_hii, mod_temp, mod_temp_precip)) ``` ::: ::: {.fragment} Have a look at the averaged coefficients ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} coefficients(mod_avg) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) log(Plot_Area) avg_temp_annual_c rain_annual_mm -2.5267209876 0.4876844180 0.0279748056 0.0000782252 hii 0.0133591861 ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Package *MuMIn* does this for us! Look at a similar table of AIC, $\Delta$AIC, and weights ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mod_avg$msTable ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` df logLik AICc delta weight 134 5 -1143.968 2298.052 0.00000 9.997160e-01 23 4 -1153.187 2314.451 16.39911 2.746982e-04 13 4 -1156.576 2321.229 23.17712 9.268898e-06 ``` ::: ::: A few things to note: - order is ranked best supported model to least supported - AICc is used instead of AIC ::: {.fragment} AICc is a sample size corrected version AIC, not a bad idea to use ::: ## Package *MuMIn* does this for us! You can get AICc with the `AICc` function from *MuMIn* ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # uncorrected AIC AIC(mod_temp_precip) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2297.937 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # sample size corrected AICc(mod_temp_precip) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 2298.052 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} Our sample size is *large*, so the correction is small ::: ## Package *MuMIn* does other things *MuMIn* lets us do some things we maybe shouldn't ::: {.incremental} - make all possible models with all possible variables - then let AIC pick one, or average over all of them - not recommended because we're just kind of "fishing" for something "significant" rather than testing hypotheses based in ecology/evolution/conservation - *MuMIn* knows its bad, their function for this workflow is called `dredge` ::: ## Package *MuMIn* does other things But `dredge`-ing can be useful for identifying which variables in our data are most "meaningful" ::: {.incremental} - `dredge` up all models - for each variable, sum up the weights of the models it is a part of - normalize those summed weights to be [0, 1] - the higher the summed weight, the more "important" that variable - should do this based on variables of interest biologically, not just every variable you could possibly get your hands on :::: ## Package *MuMIn* does other things Variable importance via summed weights ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # model with all possible variables mod_big <- glm.nb( nspp ~ log(Plot_Area) + hii + avg_temp_annual_c + rain_annual_mm, data = dat_plt, na.action = "na.fail" ) # dredge it big_dredge <- dredge(mod_big) sw(big_dredge) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` log(Plot_Area) rain_annual_mm hii avg_temp_annual_c Sum of weights: 1.00 1.00 0.99 0.45 N containing models: 8 8 8 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment} So area is important (no surprise). But a new insight: human impact and rain are quite important, and temperature less so ::: ## References

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
